# Response to the editor and reviewer


We thank the editor and reviewer for their careful reading and constructive recommendations. We revised the manuscript and tutorial code throughout. Below, we reproduce each comment and describe the corresponding change.

## Main comments

> (1) The tutorial currently describes what each code chunk does, but lacks any discussion of the meaning of the output. For example, page 10 shows code for estimating a lagged exposure model, together with the model's estimates. The tutorial should also describe how to interpret these estimates (i.e., what do they mean? what do they tell us about diffusion in these data?).

We agree. We substantially expanded the section “Fitting a lagged exposure model.” Before estimating the models, we now also correct the Korean Family Planning data's terminal time category: period 11 assigns adoption to every respondent who had not adopted earlier, rather than recording a regular observation wave. We recode the 51 terminal cases in villages 2 and 21 as right-censored and use the `diffnet` subsetting method to retain periods 1–10. This prevents the forced terminal adoptions from biasing the analysis. The revised section explains that logistic-regression coefficients are on the log-odds scale and translates the principal estimates into odds ratios. In the baseline model, a 0.10 increase in lagged cohesive exposure is associated with approximately 6% higher odds of adoption, although the estimate is not statistically distinguishable from no association ($p = 0.107$). In the adjusted model, a 0.10 increase in age-homophilic exposure corresponds to an estimated odds ratio of 1.03, each additional year of age to an odds ratio of 1.06, and residence in village 21 to an odds ratio of 0.50 relative to village 2. We also report the joint test of the period indicators, which is not statistically significant after removing the artificial terminal period ($p = 0.72$).

> (2) The code chunks frequently yield warnings that are not mentioned in the tutorial, and that do not appear in the R output displayed in the tutorial. If readers are following along, this might lead them to think something has gone wrong, but would not provide any guidance about what has gone wrong. Ideally the tutorial would be constructed so that it can run without generating any warnings. If some warnings are unavoidable, they should be explicitly discussed in the text.

We agree. We revised the examples so that readers no longer encounter unexplained warnings. Before calling `survey_to_diffnet()`, the tutorial now explicitly converts the identifier, village, and adoption-time variables to integers, eliminating the earlier coercion warnings. The structural-equivalence example explicitly specifies a valued graph and suppresses a known internal `Matrix` deprecation warning after explaining why it is benign. The static-graph warning is displayed and explained where it first occurs. In the multi-adoption section, the expected message and integer-coercion warning are displayed and explained once; subsequent repetitions are suppressed explicitly. We also explain the warning about omitting `per` from the baseline regression.

> (3) A glance at the `diffreg` function looks like it calls an ordinary general linear model (GLM). Normally it would not be appropriate to estimate a GLM on network data because these data violate the assumption that each observation (here, nodes' adoption status) is independent. It would be helpful to clarify how the logistic regression is estimated by `diffreg` to avoid this issue.

We clarified this point in detail. `diffreg()` expands the data into person-period observations, retains individuals only while they are at risk of adoption, and calls `glm()` to estimate a discrete-time logistic model. A bare `exposure` term is lagged one period by default, so adoption at time $t$ is predicted by network exposure at time $t-1$ rather than by contemporaneous adoption among contacts. Consequently, one person's adoption at time $t$ is not used to predict another person's adoption at that same time. Under the usual conditional-independence assumptions of the specified logistic regression, standard GLM inference applies; using a network-derived predictor does not by itself violate those assumptions. As in other regression analyses, fixed effects, random effects, or other adjustments can be added when warranted by the research design. The revised manuscript now states these assumptions directly and no longer incorrectly describes the default `diffreg()` model as unlagged.

> (4) Much of the manuscript describes functions that were added in netdiffuseR version 1.24.0. However, the most recent version available from CRAN is version 1.22.6, which itself has pending issues. It will be important that the version of the package described in this tutorial is available, and does not have issues pending on CRAN.

The multi-adoption and disadoption features were introduced in netdiffuseR version 1.23.0; the reference to version 1.24.0 in the original submission was a typo. The current CRAN release is now version 1.25.0, and the CRAN check-results page reports OK status across all listed platforms as of August 5, 2026. We updated the manuscript and package citation to identify version 1.25.0 as the version used while retaining 1.23.0 as the version in which these features were introduced. The current package and check results are available at <https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=netdiffuseR> and <https://CRAN.R-project.org/web/checks/check_results_netdiffuseR.html>.

## Detailed comments:

> Page 2 - I think the current definition of thresholds -- "the proportion or number of adopters in one's network when an individual adopts" -- is a bit ambiguous. This could be read as defining a threshold as purely descriptive...however many adopters were in a person's network when they happened to adopt. But, I think a threshold is usually defined as prospective...once the number of adopters in a person's network reaches the threshold, then the person will adopt themselves. It's a subtle difference, but might be worth clarifying.

We revised the definition to be prospective: a network threshold is now defined as the number or proportion of adopters required for an individual to adopt. We also distinguish the latent threshold from observed exposure at adoption and explain how interval-based observation can make exposure overstate the threshold. We added Berry et al. as a reference for this opacity problem.

> Page 3 - In the first line of the "The netdiffuseR package" section, there seems to be a broken reference with the key 'netdiffuser_2'.

We corrected the bibliography entry, verified that the citation renders, and updated it to netdiffuseR version 1.25.0 (2026).

> Page 3 - Later in the manuscript you write function names (e.g., survey_to_diffnet) in a monospaced font so they're easy to identify in the text. I'd start doing that here.

We standardized references to named R functions using monospaced type and parentheses, for example, `survey_to_diffnet()`, `exposure()`, and `rdiffnet()`.

> Page 4 - I really appreciated that you provided the QMD file with this paper. I'd suggest you put this file in a repository (GitHub, OSF, etc.) and provide a link at the beginning of the tutorial section. While it's easy enough to cut-and-paste code from the manuscript, making the QMD file easy for readers to locate would be even better.

We added a link at the beginning of the tutorial to the public repository containing `paper.qmd` and the materials needed to reproduce the manuscript: <https://github.com/gvegayon/netdiffuser-connections>.

> Page 4 - The first code chunk should also include the code necessary to install netdiffuseR. This presumably is install.packages("netdiffuseR"), however the CRAN version is 1.22.6, but this paper discusses version 1.24.0.

We added `install.packages("netdiffuseR")` before the first call to `library(netdiffuseR)` and explain that installation is required only once, whereas `library()` loads the package in each new R session.

> Page 4 - I really liked the inset "tip" box. This renders nicely in QMD, but I'm not sure how it will look once typeset for Connections, so be sure to watch for this and reformat as needed.

Thank you. We retained the tip callouts and verified their appearance in the rendered PDF. We will also work with the journal during typesetting if its production format requires a different treatment.

> Page 5 - The code chunk using `survey_to_diffnet()` yields a series of warnings coercing variables into integers. Is it possible to suppress these warnings in the function, or modify the example data so the warnings don't occur?

We eliminated these warnings by converting `id`, `village`, and `toa` explicitly with `as.integer()` before calling `survey_to_diffnet()`. The accompanying text explains why this conversion is appropriate and that it does not change the values.

> Page 5 - Enclosing `kfam_diffnet` in `print()` isn't strictly necessary because `print` is the default if `kfam_diffnet` is entered without an enclosing function. This is convenient. However, I'd suggest including it in the code here so that it is formally parallel to `summary(kfam_diffnet)` and `plot(kfam_diffnet)` in the next code chunks.

We now call `print(kfam_diffnet)` explicitly and note in the code comment that `print()` is not required in an interactive R session.

> Page 7 - You set a random number seed later in the code chunks. However, it might be useful to set this at the beginning of the tutorial so that the plot is also reproducible.

We now call `set.seed(33)` immediately before `plot_diffnet(kfam_diffnet)` and explain that the seed makes the stochastic network layout reproducible. We also set explicit seeds before the later simulation examples.

> Page 8 - Running `exp_se <- exposure(kfam_diffnet, alt.graph = "se")` gave a warning about a depricated use of as() somewhere in this function.

This is an internal compatibility warning generated by the interaction with some versions of the `Matrix` package; it does not change the calculated exposure. The revised example supplies `valued = TRUE`, suppresses the known internal deprecation warning explicitly, and explains the reason in the surrounding text. We removed the outdated promise that it would necessarily be fixed in the next package release.

> Page 8 - The LaTeX expression `$n x$` isn't rendering correctly.

We corrected the expression to $n \times T$ and define $n$ as the number of nodes and $T$ as the number of time points.

> Page 8/9 - There's a lot going on in this code chunk, and I had a hard time following the steps. It might be helpful to unpack this a bit more. In addition, the `exposure` function gives a warning about when -alt.graph- is static. Since this warning might be unexpected for readers, it might be worth commenting on it.

We reorganized this material into separate steps: creating an age-distance graph, inspecting it, transforming distance into the finite similarity weight $1/(1+d)$ on observed ties, and passing the resulting graph to `exposure()`. This revision also ensures that equal-age ties receive the maximum weight rather than being omitted. The manuscript displays and explains the warning that a static alternative graph is repeated across all time points.

> Page 9 - The `diffreg` function appears to call an ordinary glm. However, a glm assumes that the observations (here, each node's adoption status) is independent. This assumption seems to obviously be violated in this context. How does the model implemented by `diffreg` handle this?

As described in our response to main comment 3, `diffreg()` fits a discrete-time logistic regression to the at-risk person-period data and lags a bare `exposure` term by one period automatically. Under the model's conditional-independence assumptions, the regression can be estimated with standard GLM inference. The revised manuscript now explains this behavior and its assumptions immediately before interpreting the model output.

> Page 10 - The `diffreg` function yields a warning about the variable `per`. I'm not sure what this means, so it might be worth commenting on. Several other code chunks after this point also yield various warnings. I don't mention them each time, but I encourage you to either (1) write the example code so that it doesn't generate warnings, or (2) mention and explain the warnings in the tutorial. Otherwise readers may think something has gone wrong, but won't understand what.

We now explain that `per` represents the period-specific baseline adoption hazard. Because adoption prevalence and exposure both evolve over time, omitting `per` can attribute a common time trend to exposure. The baseline model retains the warning as a teaching example; the adjusted model includes `factor(per)`. We also display a joint likelihood-ratio test showing that the period indicators matter collectively. Expected warnings and messages in all later simulation chunks are either explained where first encountered or suppressed explicitly after that explanation.

> Page 13 - The most recent version of netdiffuseR on CRAN is 1.22.6, so I wasn't able to evaluate the new functions that are described as added in version 1.24.0.

As described in our response to main comment 4, the multi-adoption and disadoption functions introduced in version 1.23.0 are now available in the current CRAN release, version 1.25.0. All listed CRAN checks currently report OK status. The tutorial states the version used, and the package bibliography entry has been updated accordingly.
